passage: Looking back, I should have noticed sooner. I'm Kashish. Last winter my best friend Parul stopped coming to the canteen. She said she wasn't hungry. She stopped answering my messages for days, then sent long ones at 3 am saying she felt like a burden. I thought she was just in a mood. But it went on for weeks. One day she said, "Nothing feels worth doing anymore," and my stomach dropped. I didn't know what to say. That evening I told my mother, who told me I did the right thing. Together we spoke to our class teacher, who called Parul's parents and the school counsellor. Parul was angry with me for a while. Now she says she's glad I told.

qa.q: At what time did Parul send long messages?
qa.a: She sent long messages at 3 am.

qa.q: What made Kashish's stomach drop?
qa.a: Parul saying nothing felt worth doing made Kashish realise Parul's sadness was serious and not just a passing mood.

qa.q: What was the right thing Kashish did?
qa.a: Kashish told a parent that evening and then the class teacher, so trusted adults and the counsellor could step in, instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: Why might Parul have been angry at first?
qa.a: She may have felt exposed or embarrassed that others knew, before she felt the relief of getting help. 🤍

grounding: A teen looks back on noticing a friend's persistent sadness and withdrawal and reaching out to trusted adults.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9:
For about a month, I noticed that Dolma, usually talkative, had gone quiet. She sat at the back, stopped raising her hand, and her notebooks were half empty. Her friend Samir mentioned she'd been skipping football, which she loved. I asked her after class if things were okay. She said, "Just tired." I didn't push, but I told her my door was open and gave her the school counsellor's hours.
Two days later Dolma came to me. She said she'd been feeling sad all the time and couldn't explain why. I listened, then walked with her to the counsellor. With her permission, we informed her parents.
Follow-up: Dolma is meeting the counsellor weekly. She laughed in class today.

qa.q: Who told the teacher Dolma had been skipping football?
qa.a: Her friend Samir told the teacher.

qa.q: What does Dolma's reply "Just tired" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she wasn't ready to explain her sadness yet and may have felt unsure or ashamed to open up.

qa.q: Which of the teacher's steps helped Dolma most, and why?
qa.a: The teacher noticed changes over time, offered help without pushing and shared the counsellor's hours, so Dolma could come forward when ready and be walked to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Samir feel knowing Dolma is getting help?
qa.a: Samir may feel relieved that the worry was taken seriously and that Dolma is starting to feel better.

grounding: A teacher's note shows noticing persistent sadness and withdrawal in a student and helping her reach a professional.

passage:
Sunday night
I've felt weird for weeks. Not sad exactly, just heavy, and my chest gets tight before school every morning. Today I skipped Binita's birthday because I couldn't face people. That's not me. I used to love parties.
I searched online about it, and the pages said a lot of scary things that made me feel worse. So I stopped.
Binita texted: "Missed u. U ok?" I almost wrote "yes" but I wrote "not really." She said to talk to someone older.
So I'm going to tell Bade Papa tomorrow. He's calm and doesn't make things into a drama. My hands shake just writing this. But I think I need someone to help me work out what's happening.
Harish

qa.q: Whose birthday did Harish skip?
qa.a: Harish skipped Binita's birthday.

qa.q: How is Harish feeling while writing this entry?
qa.a: Harish feels heavy and anxious, with a tight chest before school, and scared enough to shake at the thought of telling someone.

qa.q: Why is telling Bade Papa a better step than searching online?
qa.a: The online pages made Harish feel worse, while a calm trusted adult can listen and help Harish reach proper help.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling when Harish replies "not really"?
qa.a: She is probably worried but also glad Harish was honest, which is why she encourages Harish to talk to someone older.

grounding: A teen's diary shows Harish recognising weeks of anxiety and withdrawal and deciding to reach a trusted adult.

passage: Since the results in April, Kiran, fifteen, had stopped going to the fields in the evenings with the other girls. She sat on the charpai and stared at the tamarind tree. Her mother said she was lazy. Weeks passed like that. One afternoon at the handpump, her friend Salma said, 'You don't even laugh at my jokes. Are you okay?' Kiran felt her eyes fill. 'I feel heavy all the time. Even when nothing is wrong.' Salma held her hand. 'This has been going on too long, Kiran. Let's tell Sister Mercy at school. She knows about these things.' The next day, Sister Mercy listened and said, 'Thank you for telling me. There's a counsellor at the district hospital. We'll talk to your mother together.'

qa.q: Where did Salma talk to Kiran?
qa.a: At the handpump.

qa.q: How did Kiran describe what she was feeling?
qa.a: She said she felt heavy all the time, even when nothing was wrong.

qa.q: Why was Salma's suggestion a good one?
qa.a: She noticed it had lasted a long time and linked Kiran to a trusted adult who could get proper help.

qa.q: How might Kiran's mother see the situation after the meeting?
qa.a: She might realise that what she called laziness was real distress that needed care, not scolding.

grounding: Shows a rural teen recognising persistent sadness and withdrawal and reaching out to trusted adults and a counsellor.

passage:
In Toronto, Hana, sixteen, noticed that her friend Nour hadn't eaten lunch for two weeks. Nour stopped coming to the robotics club, sat with her hood up, and when Hana asked, she said, “I'm just tired. Nothing feels fun any more.”
It didn't pass. Hana felt worried in her stomach.
On Friday, she said, “Nour, I think this is more than tired. Can we go to Ms Chen together?”
Nour shook her head, then shrugged. “If you come.”
They went to the school counsellor at lunch. Ms Chen listened, thanked Nour for coming, and asked her gently about sleep and feelings. She called Nour's parents that afternoon and set up a weekly meeting.
Walking out, Nour said quietly, “Thanks for noticing.”

qa.q: What had Nour stopped coming to?
qa.a: The robotics club.

qa.q: How did Hana feel about Nour's changes?
qa.a: Hana felt worried, noticing the sadness and withdrawal had lasted weeks.

qa.q: What did Hana do that was helpful, and why?
qa.a: She named her worry kindly and went with Nour to the counsellor, so a trusted professional could help.

qa.q: How did Ms Chen respond when Nour came in?
qa.a: She listened, thanked Nour, asked gently about sleep and feelings, and called her parents that afternoon.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old recognises a friend's lasting withdrawal and helps her reach a counsellor.

passage:
For six weeks, Jahnavi, fifteen, had felt heavy. She woke up tired, stopped enjoying dance, and cried in the hostel bathroom where no one would see.
She told herself it was exam stress. But exams had ended a month ago.
One night she looked at the poster by the warden's office: Feeling low for weeks? Talk to someone. She read it three times.
The next morning, she knocked on the school counsellor's door. “Uday Sir, I don't know what's wrong. I just feel sad all the time.”
Mr Uday closed his notebook and pulled up a chair. “Thank you for coming. That took courage. Tell me when it started.”
She talked for forty minutes. He called her parents, with her permission, and they agreed she would see him every week, and a doctor if needed.

qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: How was Jahnavi feeling before she went to the counsellor?

qa.q: What made Jahnavi's decision to seek help wise?

Okay, so you asked why I care so much about mental health. I'm Rashmi, and it started with my friend Harish in Class 10.
For weeks he stopped coming for cricket. He said he was tired. He stopped replying in the group chat. At lunch he just moved his food around. He said, "What's the point of anything?"

I'm Omkar. Sahil's been my best friend since Class 5. This term, something changed.

For six weeks, Rashmi had felt flat. Not sad about anything; just grey. She stopped drawing, cried in the shower, and lay awake. She'd read about this in a health poster at school: when it keeps going for weeks, tell someone.
The problem was timing. It was exam week, her parents were at a family wedding in another city, and the school counsellor only came on Tuesdays. It was Thursday.
She almost decided to wait. Instead, that evening, she called her aunt Nazia, who lived across town. "I think something's wrong with me. I've been feeling bad for weeks."
Nazia didn't brush it off. She came over within the hour, stayed the night, and called Rashmi's parents with her. Next morning she rang the school and booked the counsellor for Tuesday, and a family doctor for Saturday.

qa.q: How long had Rashmi felt flat?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she almost decided to wait?
qa.a: Rashmi felt tired and unsure, tempted to wait because everything seemed badly timed.

qa.q: Why was calling Nazia the right step despite the bad timing?
qa.a: Because the feeling had lasted weeks, and a trusted adult could act straight away and connect Rashmi to her parents, the counsellor and a doctor.

qa.a: They were likely worried and sad not to be there, but relieved that Rashmi told someone and wasn't alone.

In the lunch break at their Kolkata school, Alka noticed Hansa had stopped laughing at anything. For weeks Hansa had skipped their walks, her nails were bitten raw, and she kept saying, "I just can't breathe properly before tests."
Today Hansa hadn't opened her tiffin again.
Alka sat next to her. "You don't seem okay. For a long time now."
Hansa's eyes filled up. "I'm scared all the time. I don't know why. Please don't make it a big thing."
"I think it is a big thing, and that's okay," Alka said. "Can we tell Ms Ghosh together? Now?"
Hansa nodded after a while. They went to the staffroom before the bell. Ms Ghosh listened, took them to the counsellor's room and called Hansa's mother that afternoon to come in.

qa.a: Hansa hadn't opened her tiffin.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she told Alka?
qa.a: Hansa felt scared all the time, and anxious about it being made into a big thing.

qa.a: Her mother might feel worried and a little shocked, but relieved the school noticed and brought her in.
